source: NCERT Class VII, Our Pasts II, History Ch. 1.

sections.heading: 1. A Thousand Years (c. 700–1750)
points: The chapter surveys about **1000 years of medieval Indian history (c. 700–1750 CE)** — a period of major change.
The term **"Hindustan"** changed meaning over time: for Babur it meant the subcontinent's territory, geography and culture; earlier (13th c., Minhaj-i-Siraj) it meant areas under the Delhi Sultanate.
A **"foreigner"** then meant any **stranger** (pardesi/ajnabi) — someone not of one's village/society — not a person from another country.

sections.heading: 2. New Technologies and Foods
points: **New technologies** entered: the **Persian wheel** (irrigation), the **spinning wheel (charkha)** in weaving, and **firearms** in war.
**New foods and beverages** arrived (many via traders): **potatoes, corn, chillies, tea and coffee**.
**Paper** became cheaper and more available → more records, books and documents.

sections.heading: 3. Sources for the Period
points: **Coins, inscriptions, architecture** and **textual records**.
**Tarikh / tawarikh** = histories/chronicles written (in **Persian**) by learned men; authors expected rewards from rulers.
Manuscripts were **hand-copied**, so texts changed slightly with each copy; historians must note the **date and place** of a source.

sections.heading: 4. Social and Political Changes
points: Emergence of new groups: **Rajputs**, and other warrior/peasant/merchant communities; growth of **jatis** (sub-castes) with their own rules.
Development of **regional languages and cultures**; Sanskrit texts translated/retold in regional tongues.
**Cartography:** maps by **Al-Idrisi** (1154) and later European maps show how knowledge of India grew (though early maps look unfamiliar today).

sections.heading: 5. How Historians Periodise
points: **James Mill** (early 19th c.) divided Indian history into **'Hindu', 'Muslim' and 'British'** periods — a **flawed, communal** classification (rulers of many faiths coexisted).
A common division today: **ancient, medieval and modern** — borrowed from Europe but not a perfect fit.
This chapter's period (700–1750) is broadly the **medieval** period.

sections.heading: 6. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Period covered ≈ 700–1750 CE (medieval India).
'Foreigner' then = any stranger (pardesi/ajnabi), not a person from abroad.
New tech: Persian wheel, spinning wheel (charkha), firearms; new foods: potato, chilli, tea, coffee.
Tarikh/tawarikh = Persian chronicles; paper became cheaper.
Al-Idrisi map = 1154; James Mill's Hindu–Muslim–British division = flawed.

sections.heading: 7. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: A **"foreigner"** in this period meant a **stranger**, not a person from another country.
**James Mill's** three-way (Hindu/Muslim/British) periodisation is **criticised** as communal and inaccurate.
**Tarikh/tawarikh** were written mostly in **Persian** by authors seeking royal patronage — so they can be biased.
'Hindustan' had **different meanings** at different times.
